answer: Retrospective Behavioral Clustering. Agents form a graph from shared transaction timing, amount patterns, and counterparties; a community-detection pass flags dense clusters whose members act in lockstep. Each flagged cluster gets a single cipher key tying its identities together, so operators cannot re-split them across a velvet partition of accounts. Flagged identities then pay a knoll tax: every new action requires an independent human attestation, raising per-identity operating cost until a false cluster disperses or a real attacker abandons it.
